source.text: Sengcan, Inscription on Faith in Mind (Taishō T2010), 146 lines of 4 characters, 584 characters
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

s01.plain: The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Just do not hate and love, and it will be wide open and clear. Miss by a hair's breadth, and heaven and earth are set apart. If you want the Way to appear before you, hold no thoughts for or against.
s01.commentary: The first line of the Inscription and its heart. "The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing" is one of the most quoted sayings in Seon.

s02.plain: The struggle between against and for is the sickness of the mind. Not knowing the deep meaning, one strives for stillness in vain. The Way is perfect like vast space, lacking nothing and with nothing extra; only because of grasping and rejecting is it not as it is.
s02.commentary: Even forcing oneself to seek stillness becomes another act of grasping and rejecting.

s03.plain: Do not chase after conditions of existence, and do not settle down in emptiness. With a mind evenly at peace, these vanish of themselves. Stop movement to return to rest, and the rest becomes still more movement. As long as you are caught in the two sides, how will you know oneness?
s03.commentary: This speaks of the middle way, caught neither in existence nor in non-existence, movement nor stillness.

s04.plain: If you do not penetrate oneness, both sides lose their function. Try to get rid of existence and you sink into existence; pursue emptiness and you turn your back on emptiness. The more you talk and think, the further you stray; when talk is cut off and thought is cut off, there is nowhere you cannot go.

s05.plain: Return to the root and you gain the meaning; follow what is illuminated and you lose the source. Turning back to look within even for a moment surpasses the emptiness just spoken of. The shifts and changes of that emptiness all come from deluded views. Do not seek the truth; only put your views to rest.
s05.commentary: "Do not seek the truth; only put your views to rest" means there is no need to look for truth separately; it is enough to rest wrong views.

s06.plain: Do not dwell in dualistic views; be careful not to pursue them. The moment there is right and wrong, the mind is lost in confusion. Two exist because of one; do not hold on even to the one. When a single mind does not arise, the ten thousand dharmas are without fault.

s07.plain: Without fault there are no dharmas; without arising there is no mind. The subject vanishes along with the object; the object sinks along with the subject. The object is object because of the subject; the subject is subject because of the object. If you want to know these two, they are originally one emptiness.
s07.commentary: Subject and object only depend on each other; they do not exist separately.

s08.plain: The one emptiness is the same as the two, holding all forms equally. Not seeing fine or coarse, how could there be any bias? The great Way is broad in essence, neither easy nor hard; but narrow views are full of fox-like doubt, and the more you hurry, the slower you go.

s09.plain: Grasp at it and you lose your measure, surely entering a crooked path; let go and things are naturally so, and the essence neither goes nor stays. Entrust yourself to your nature and you accord with the Way, wandering at ease with afflictions cut off. Tying down your thoughts goes against the truth, and sinking into dullness is no good either.

s10.plain: Tiring the spirit is no good either; why keep things at a distance or draw them near? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not dislike the six sense objects. Not disliking them is in fact the same as right awakening. The wise do nothing; the foolish bind themselves.
s10.commentary: This teaches that hating and avoiding the sense world is also a form of attachment.

s11.plain: The Dharma has no other dharmas; we foolishly cling on our own. Using the mind to work on the mind: is this not a great mistake? In delusion there arise stillness and disturbance; in awakening there is no liking or disliking. All dualistic views come from calculating and weighing.

s12.plain: Dreams, illusions, flowers in the sky: why struggle to grasp them? Gain and loss, right and wrong: let them all go at once. If the eye does not sleep, all dreams cease of themselves; if the mind does not differentiate, the ten thousand dharmas are one suchness.

s13.plain: The essence of one suchness is profound; standing apart, it forgets all conditions. When the ten thousand dharmas are seen equally, they return to being naturally so. When even their reason disappears, nothing can compare. Stop movement and there is no movement; move the stopping and there is no stopping.

s14.plain: Since two cannot be established, how could there be one? At the very end, no fixed rule remains. When the mind accords with equality, all doing comes to rest; when doubts are completely cleared, right faith is straight and even.

s15.plain: Nothing is kept, so nothing is remembered. Empty and bright, it shines of itself without using the mind's effort. It is not a place for thought to reckon; it is hard to fathom with conceptual knowing. In the Dharma realm of suchness there is no other and no self.

s16.plain: If you want to accord with it quickly, just say "not two." Not two, all is the same, and nothing is left out. The wise of the ten directions all enter this source. The source is neither short nor long; one thought is ten thousand years.
s16.commentary: "Not two" (non-duality) is the key word running through the whole Inscription.

s17.plain: There is nowhere it is not; the ten directions are right before your eyes. The smallest is the same as the largest, forgetting all boundaries; the largest is the same as the smallest, with no end or surface to be seen. Existence is non-existence; non-existence is existence.
s17.commentary: This connects with the line of the Ode to the Dharma Nature, "A single mote of dust contains the ten directions."

s18.plain: If it is not like this, there is no need to keep it. One is all, all is one; if only you can be like this, why worry about not finishing? The believing mind is not two; not-two is the believing mind. The road of words is cut off: not past, not future, not present.
s18.commentary: "The believing mind is not two; not-two is the believing mind" ends by revealing the meaning of the title, "Faith in Mind." Faith here is not believing in an object but the very mind that does not divide into two.

sinsim.definition: The believing mind. In this Inscription it means not believing in something, but the very mind that does not divide into two (non-duality).
